DecSummary: The worker was entitled to a permanent disability reassessment for his bilateral wrist condition. The Board denied a reassessment on the basis that there was insufficient evidence of a significant deterioration, worsening, or change in the worker's condition. Tribunal case law has consistently held that the test of 'significant deterioration' that triggers a NEL re-determination is not applicable to permanent disability reassessments. Rather, the test under the applicable policy is whether there is a permanent worsening in the worker's condition, which means a worsening that is more than trivial or de minimus. The evidence indicated that the worker had a permanent worsening of his condition.

DecSummary: This appeal was referred to the Tribunal's Early Intervention Process. The issue on appeal was the  worker's entitlement to a recalculation of his LOE benefits from December 20, 2002 based on an ability to work 20 hours per week, in the SEB of Other Elemental Service Occupations, at minimum wage. The Vice-Chair noted the worker's age, low education level, failed attempts at retraining, and his lack of transferrable skills as well as the medical information on file regarding deteriorating compensable conditions and surgeries. The worker had extensive physical restrictions that would likely limit his job options. The worker's treating physician stated as far back as 2003, that the worker would have had problems returning to full-time work. Part-time work at a minimum wage elemental service job was therefore an appropriate basis for the worker's LOE award.

The Vice-Chair accepted a proposed resolution developed through the early intervention process rating the NEL award at 20%. The NEL assessment was based on an April 2019 report from a psychiatrist. DecKeywords: Permanent impairment {NEL} (degree of impairment) (knee); Apportionment (non-economic loss) (preexisting conditions)
DecSummary: The worker's appeal of a reduction in the NEL award for his knee for a pre-existing condition was allowed. An asymptomatic pre-existing condition should not be deducted or factored out when determining a NEL rating. Board policy requires that the evidence must show that the pre-existing condition on its own would result in an impairment rating under the AMA Guides. There is no language indicating that an asymptomatic pre-existing condition is a basis for reducing the quantum of a NEL award. As the worker's condition was asymptomatic and would not attract any impairment rating or alternatively would be rated at zero, the worker was entitled to the NEL award without reduction.
